articleTitle: The potential of brushless doubly-fed machines for adjustable speed drives
publicationTitle: Annual Technical Conference on Pulp and Paper Industry
abstract: The more widespread adoption of adjustable-speed drives to promote process efficiency through energy conservation is currently hampered by the high cost of power electronic conversion units for use with AC motors. The examination of alternative methods of obtaining speed control in both synchronous and induction machines leads to the conclusion that a self-cascaded machine has considerable promise. The motor has six input terminals to the same stator windings: one three-phase set presenting a different pole number to the other three-phase set. The rotor is a specialized form of a robust cage construction without slip rings. When operated in a doubly-fed mode, this machine requires only a fraction of its input power to be processed by a power electronic converter. The resulting system has the potential to provide a low cost, robust, fault-tolerant, precise speed, and adjustable speed drive.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Tin plating versus silver plating and the use of silver alloys on electrical equipment for the paper industry
publicationTitle: Annual Technical Conference on Pulp and Paper Industry
abstract: The use of tin plating versus silver plating and the use of silver alloys on electrical equipment in the paper industry are addressed. The advantages and disadvantages of tin and silver are reviewed. The evolution from silver to tin plating in one paper mill is discussed, the results are reviewed. Examples are cited of failures in the mill where silver was used for electrical contacts and where silver alloys were used for joining electrical components into assemblies.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Investigation and results of eddy currents on DC motor bearings
publicationTitle: Annual Technical Conference on Pulp and Paper Industry
abstract: Investigation into several similar bearing failures has led to the realization that the source of electrical current causing the failures is not fully understood and that the problem is widespread. Probable causes, an attempt to measure the currents, and possible solutions to the bearing failure are discussed. Several methods of bearing fluting due to eddy currents in the shaft of DC machines are discussed, and procedures to avoid applying the currents or to protect the machine from the currents are outlined. It is noted that there is no conclusive evidence that defines a cure for the problem of capacitive coupled eddy currents in the motor shaft; however, until the problem is better defined and a correction made, drive installations with 13.8 kV primary voltage on isolation transformers with multiple drives would do well to apply shaft grounding brushes to reduce the occurrence of fluted bearings on machines.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Overload protection for medium voltage motors controlled by switchgear starters
publicationTitle: Annual Technical Conference on Pulp and Paper Industry
abstract: The author addresses the application of traditional types of overload protective devices, notes some of the difficulties in doing so, and then recommends the better types. It is suggested that a combination of relays may be the best answer. Microprocessor relays, with good memory characteristics, are probably the best protection that can be applied, but they must be studied closely to be properly set. Some of them are furnished with the possibility of custom-building the protection curve. It is noted that this is much easier then to fit the curve including overload, start, and stall protection between the motor start run curve and the motor thermal withstand curve, which is the ultimate overload protection.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Networking communication for power monitoring, protection and control of mill power distribution
publicationTitle: Annual Technical Conference on Pulp and Paper Industry
abstract: The use of local area networks to monitor, protect, and control a paper mill power system is described. Types of equipment that can be monitored and information that is transmitted and recorded, installations in paper mill applications, hardware that is added to form local area networks, and how the information is transmitted are considered.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Collector ring marking or brush footprinting
publicationTitle: Annual Technical Conference on Pulp and Paper Industry
abstract: Collector ring marking, also known as brush footprinting or photographing, has been a persistent problem for many years on carbon-brush collectors of synchronous machines from different manufacturers. The theory that the footprints are formed by simultaneous loss of electrical contact of all brushes on the ring is proposed. The trigger for the loss of contact is mechanical, but adverse ring film conditions, such as oil contamination, can greatly accelerate the appearance of the marks. The test results which led to the loss-of-contact theory are explained, and corrective steps, as well as their efficacy, are described. In particular, modifications consisting of increased spring pressure, more brushes, greater peripheral brush spacing, and stiffer brushholder supports where needed were devised to eliminate or minimize simultaneous loss of brush contact.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Retrofitting obsolete 15 kV switchgear for a pulp and paper mill
publicationTitle: Annual Technical Conference on Pulp and Paper Industry
abstract: A case study involving the resolution of certain engineering and logistical problems encountered in upgrading existing obsolete 15 kV 750 MVA air magnetic switchgear to meet a 1000 MVA application at an integrated pulp and paper mill is presented. The existing 15 kV switchgear is essential to the mill's operation, and could not be shut down for construction purposes. The solution was to utilize a retrofitting technique. The technique involves removing the existing circuit breaker element from its cubicle and stripping off everything associated with the old breaker. The stripped breaker element frame is refitted with state-of-the-art vacuum interrupters. The retrofitted assembly is reinserted into the existing cubicle and placed into service. The mill site application requirements, the selection of a qualified retrofitter, the retrofitting procedure, the benefits of retrofitting and the testing and installation experience are described.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Application of an AC winder drive
publicationTitle: Annual Technical Conference on Pulp and Paper Industry
abstract: The first major installation of AC adjustable speed drive technology in North America was in 1987 on a Kraft linerboard machine at Union Camp Corporation's (UCC) Savannah, GA, papermill. The success of that installation led to the application of AC drive technology to a high-speed electric backstand winder in the UCC Savannah mill in 1988-9. This AC winder drive project is described in detail, with attention given to engineering, construction, and shutdown. It is noted that, since start-up of the winder drive system in April 1989, there have been no problems relative to the drive control systems.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Analysis of ground potential gradients around power substations
publicationTitle: Annual Technical Conference on Pulp and Paper Industry
abstract: The substation ground potential rise due to a primary single-line-to-ground fault could be as high as 20 kV. A portion of this ground potential rise could be transferred to nearby plant ground grids through the earth, even if the two grounding grids are not bonded together. The percentage of this ground potential rise transfer depends on soil resistivity, distance between the power substation and the plant, and size of the substation itself. An accurate grounding system analysis program based on a two-layer soil model has been used to develop charts to illustrate the effect of these three variables on the potential gradients outside the power substation. The charts provide a guide for estimating the potential transferred to the plant ground due to the power substation ground potential rise without it being necessary to use a computer program.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Experience with synchronous motor driven chipper drives with power factor regulation
publicationTitle: Annual Technical Conference on Pulp and Paper Industry
abstract: It is pointed out that most existing and new installations could use the inherent characteristics of synchronous chipper motors to far better advantage with the proper field regulation and control. The various control methods which are being implemented are discussed, and the deficiencies of many of these schemes are noted. The control of the synchronous motor field by power factor regulation is recommended, and field test results are discussed. It is concluded that power factor regulation has been found to be useful in chipper applications where the motors are subjected to high-level transient impact loads. The power factor regulator senses the power factor dip that occurs when the motor is loaded and causes the motor to respond with a boosted output. As a result, the pull-out torque of the synchronous motor is increased for the duration of the transient load, thus reducing the probability of pole slippage. This automatic boosting of field current is called field forcing. Thus, the power factor regulator provides automatic boosting when field forcing is required, and economical low-field operation when the motor is idling.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Effect of waveform distortion on protective relays
publicationTitle: Annual Technical Conference on Pulp and Paper Industry
abstract: The authors attempted to show, theoretically and by laboratory tests, the influence of harmonics on protective relays. Representative relays using various operating principles were tested using fundamental currents and/or voltages. They were then tested using single frequency inputs that were multiples of the fundamental frequency. Finally, tests were made using realistic combinations of fundamental and harmonics. From this series of tests, it is evident that the influence of harmonics (with magnitude decreasing with order) on the steady-state behavior of the protective relays is minor and insignificant. For faults containing a substantial DC component, the performance of the various relaying units will vary markedly depending on the duration of the DC, and more importantly on the nature of the measuring concept.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Electrical energy usage in the pulp and paper industry
publicationTitle: Annual Technical Conference on Pulp and Paper Industry
abstract: The authors examine the electrical energy usage in the pulp and paper industry for the continental United States. It is noted that the broad picture of energy required and fuel sources used gives a clear indication of a movement away from oil as an energy source. Internally generated fuel sources of spent liquor and hogged fuel have increased. The steam generated from boilers has increased internally generated electricity. It is pointed out that technologies such as high-yield pulping and impulse drying require less chemicals and reduced thermal requirements. The advanced thermal analysis technique of pinch technology focuses on optimum use of thermal requirements. It is concluded that all of these technologies point the way to more efficient thermal usage and increased demand for electricity.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Integrated approach to power systems analysis and maintenance
publicationTitle: Annual Technical Conference on Pulp and Paper Industry
abstract: An integrated approach to power systems analysis and maintenance is described. The main system element is a protective device database which can be accessed through a graphical interface module. Using this interface, users can access protective device settings, test sheet information, and generate work schedule reports. The database is also linked to internal and external short circuit and coordination modules, thus providing a unified decision support system for both plant engineers and maintenance personnel. How his system was implemented in a paper mill to improve the management of the electrical distribution system is described.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Effecting changes in the National Electrical Code
publicationTitle: Annual Technical Conference on Pulp and Paper Industry
abstract: Since new products and electrical technology are constantly evolving, it is necessary to periodically revise the National Electrical Code to incorporate these changes in materials and method. The complete revision cycle is defined, and guidance for submitting proposals to revise the National Electrical Code is provided. Sample forms are included.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Considerations for an economic evaluation of AC vs. DC technology for paper machine drives
publicationTitle: Annual Technical Conference on Pulp and Paper Industry
abstract: Many of the considerations for comparing AC and DC drive systems for paper machines are discussed. A procedure for making an economic evaluation between the two technologies is presented. Two evaluation examples are discussed. Areas of comparison include: system purchase price, spare parts costs, motor cooling factors, cable costs, power factor corrections, harmonic generation, system efficiency, maintenance, and space requirements.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Improving machine up-time through systematic electrical control design and documentation
publicationTitle: Annual Technical Conference on Pulp and Paper Industry
abstract: The author provides some ideas for a systems-oriented approach to the electrical control documents required for installation and commissioning of today's computer-intensive process lines. Each type of document conveys certain information required at each phase of a project. The author attempts to guide the reader through the design phases of a project, while providing a method and a system of electrical control documentation proven to provide a solution to controlling the costs of installation, commissioning, and ongoing maintenance.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Lockout and tagout training
publicationTitle: Annual Technical Conference on Pulp and Paper Industry
abstract: The steps in the development of a training video for lockout and tagout of electrical equipment in a large pulp and paper mill are explained. The goals and methods used to develop the training video are outlined, and some thoughts on segments that came out well and areas that could have been improved are presented. The individual steps involved in producing the video are reviewed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Setting goals and measuring performance: the challenge for engineering management
publicationTitle: Annual Technical Conference on Pulp and Paper Industry
abstract: The author discusses a method of setting goals for engineers working on large projects. The goals considered are facility performance, quality, safety and housekeeping, cost and schedule, and customer satisfaction. The author also discusses how to get feedback for hard goals which can be quantified and measured as well as for soft goals which are very subjective.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Millwide-the second time (process control system)
publicationTitle: Annual Technical Conference on Pulp and Paper Industry
abstract: In 1988 the New Bern North Carolina pulp mill implemented a millwide information system based on one developed at Weyerhaeuser's Longview Washington Complex two years earlier. In the present work, the author examines the concept of millwide, what it is, why Weyerhaeuser developed their own systems, why New Bern copied the Longview system, what advantages there were, as well as what problems were encountered. Particular attention is paid to the differences in the two implementations, both the technical and the intangibles. A brief history of the original implementation is provided, but the primary focus is on the implementation at New Bern and how millwide is being implemented and managed there.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Characteristics of different power systems neutral grounding techniques: facts and fiction
publicationTitle: Annual Technical Conference on Pulp and Paper Industry
abstract: The authors review the characteristics of different power systems grounding techniques as currently applied, and misapplied, within industry today. They note that, in many cases, misunderstood concepts and perceptions of the purpose and type of power systems grounding to be selected date back to the 1940s and earlier. Since that time much research, coupled with experience, that is now available to industry has taken place. The authors review the many different system grounding practices and present information on different grounding methods. Safety, National Electric Code requirements, and operational considerations, such as continuity of service, are investigated. Finally, examples of proper applications within various industries are given.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Application, design and rating of transformers containing harmonic currents
publicationTitle: Annual Technical Conference on Pulp and Paper Industry
abstract: Semiconductor power converters used as power supplies for both AC and DC motors produce harmonic currents which affect other types of electrical equipment. The effect of these currents on transformers used in such systems is examined here. The authors define the problem, provide guidelines for the design and rating of new transformers, and explain how to derate existing transformers that, as a result of retrofit, are now subject to harmonic currents. It is noted that transformers subject to harmonic currents from SCR circuits have higher losses due to the increased eddy current and stray losses resulting from the high-frequency components of the current. With the aid of IEEE Standard C57.110 losses can be estimated if the eddy current and stray loss components of the load losses are known under sinusoidal conditions and the harmonic spectrum of the load currents. With this information, standard kilovoltampere transformers subject to harmonic currents using hottest-spot loading as a criteria can be derated. Since this increases the losses is considered by a factor of 4, the transformer is essentially derated by a factor twice as high as would be used if average loss density were used as a criterion. It is pointed out that using transformers designed with low eddy current losses and/or circuits designed to decrease the harmonic content of the load currents will greatly minimize the effects of harmonic current on transformers.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The value of conceptual power system design studies
publicationTitle: Annual Technical Conference on Pulp and Paper Industry
abstract: An attempt is made to familiarize industrial plant engineers and power consultants with the elements of and the procedure for conducting a conceptual design study, which should be performed in the early phases of expansion and modernization projects. To contrast the differences with more familiar studies (such as short-circuit studies, etc.), an illustrative example indicating the high financial rewards involved is given. A conceptual design study involves the search for an optimum power system arrangement in which various facility-specific and system-design-specific criteria are harmoniously integrated to meet the present and future production objectives. These studies offer a credible procedure to maximize the long-range investment in an electrical power system by offering a number of system design alternatives based on and supported by a comprehensive engineering analysis of their characteristics. From this thorough examination, a final design is selected for implementation. These studies yield a rationalized alternative to the practice of designing a new system by merely duplicating a previous system design, which itself may have been derived from an earlier (and possibly obsolete) system.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: ESD in the manufacture, assembly, test, delivery, operation, and repair of distribution control system components
publicationTitle: Annual Technical Conference on Pulp and Paper Industry
abstract: The causes of ESD (electrostatic discharge) and its effects on electrical and electronic parts are examined, and ESD protective materials and equipment are discussed. Issues discussed include IC protection, the effects of surface charge density, protective transport packaging, the protective environments, and CMOS latchup. It is also concluded that everyone involved in processing, assembly, inspection, handling, packaging, shipping, storage, stowage, testing, installation, and maintenance of susceptible parts throughout the equipment life cycle, both at the manufacturer's and the user's facility, needs to be aware of the damage that can be done to ESD sensitive parts, and should be trained on how to control their environment to minimize the potential for damage.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Electrical engineering-pulp and paper bibliography 1977-89
publicationTitle: Annual Technical Conference on Pulp and Paper Industry
abstract: A bibliography of electrical engineering papers presented during the past thirteen years is arranged by subject index to provide a library base for the pulp and paper industry. The subject index covers general topics, design and construction methods, cable, lighting, codes and standards, lightning, grounding and surge protection, power systems, transformers and switchgear, protective relaying, computer analysis, process control and instrumentation systems, training and safety programs, economics, modernization, maintenance, power requirements and application data, AC motors and motor control, DC motors and drive systems (hardware), adjustable speed drives (methods), process control computers and programmable controllers, and power and recovery boiler controls.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
